{{Short description|Result in elementary number theory}}
In elementary [[number theory]], the '''lifting-the-exponent lemma''' provides several formulas for computing the [[p-adic valuation|{{mvar|p}}-adic valuation]] <math>\nu_p</math> of binomial expressions which are differences of powers of integers: that is, how many factors of a prime <math>p</math> are present. The lemma describes the steps necessary to "lift" the exponent of <math>p</math> in such expressions. It is related to [[Hensel's lemma]]. It is often used in [[mathematical olympiads]].

== History ==
By 1878, some ideas in the lemma had appeared in the work of mathematician [[Édouard Lucas]],<ref name="Lucas1878">É. Lucas, "Théorie des Fonctions Numériques Simplement Périodiques. [Continued]", ''American Journal of Mathematics'', vol. 1 (1878), pp. 197–240. https://www.jstor.org/stable/2369308</ref> who was then a professor at [[Lycée Charlemagne]]. Lucas described related divisibility results (with a minor error in the case <math>p = 2</math>).

In 2006, Romanian mathematician Mihai Manea first published the modern and systematic formulation of the lemma, especially in the context of olympiad mathematics.<ref name="Manea2006">M. Manea, "Some a^n ± b^n Problems in Number Theory", ''Mathematics Magazine'', vol. 79, no. 2, April 2006, pp. 140–145. https://web.archive.org/web/20200322064554/https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/mathmag140-145-manea44299.pdf</ref>

By 2011, the lemma had become well-known in the math olympiad folklore, particularly through its use on mathematics forums such as the [[Richard_Rusczyk#Art_of_Problem_Solving|Art of Problem Solving]].<ref name="Parvardi">Parvardi, Amir H. (2011). https://s3.amazonaws.com/aops-cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/resources/articles/lifting-the-exponent.pdf</ref>

== Statements ==
For a [[prime number]] <math>p</math>, let <math>\nu_p(x) = k</math>, where <math>p^k</math> is the highest power of <math>p</math> which is a [[divisor]] of <math>x</math>, so that <math>p^k \mid x, \ \  p^{k+1}\nmid x</math>. For any integers <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> with <math>p \nmid x</math> and <math>p \nmid y</math>, and a positive integer <math>n</math>, the following statements hold:

* When <math>p</math> is odd:
** If <math>p \mid x-y</math>, then <math>\nu_p(x^n-y^n) = \nu_p(x-y)+\nu_p(n)</math>.
** If <math>p \mid x+y</math> and <math>n</math> is odd, then <math>\nu_p(x^n+y^n) = \nu_p(x+y)+\nu_p(n)</math>.
** If <math>p \mid x+y</math> and <math>n</math> is even, then <math>\nu_p(x^n+y^n) = 0</math>.
* When <math>p = 2</math>:
** If <math>2 \mid x-y</math> and <math>n</math> is even, then <math>\nu_2(x^n-y^n) = \nu_2(x-y)+\nu_2(x+y)+\nu_2(n)-1 = \nu_2\!\left(\frac{x^2-y^2}{2}\right)+\nu_2(n)</math>.
** If <math>2 \mid x-y</math> and <math>n</math> is odd, then <math>\nu_2(x^n-y^n) = \nu_2(x-y)</math>. (Follows from the general case below.)
** Corollaries:
*** If <math>4 \mid x-y</math>, and if both <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are odd, then <math>\nu_2(x+y)=1</math> and thus <math>\nu_2(x^n-y^n) = \nu_2(x-y)+\nu_2(n)</math>.
*** If <math>2 \mid x+y</math> and <math>n</math> is even, then <math>\nu_2(x^n+y^n) = 1</math>.
*** If <math>2 \mid x+y</math> and <math>n</math> is odd, then <math>\nu_2(x^n+y^n) = \nu_2(x+y)</math>.
* For all <math>p</math>:
** If <math>p \mid x-y</math> and <math>p \nmid n</math>, then <math>\nu_p(x^n-y^n) = \nu_p(x-y)</math>.
** If <math>p \mid x+y</math>, <math>p \nmid n</math> and <math>n</math> is odd, then <math>\nu_p(x^n+y^n) = \nu_p(x+y)</math>.

== Generalizations ==

The lifting-the-exponent lemma has been generalized to complex values of <math>x, y</math> provided that the value of <math>\tfrac{x^n-y^n}{x-y}</math> is an integer.<ref>S. Riasat, [https://sriasat.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/general-lte.pdf Generalising `LTE' and application to Fibonacci-type sequences].</ref>

== Proof outline ==
=== Base case ===
The base case <math>\nu_p(x^n-y^n) = \nu_p(x-y)</math> when <math>p \nmid n</math> is proven first. Because <math>p \mid x-y \iff x \equiv y \pmod{p}</math>,
{{NumBlk|:|<math>x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}y+x^{n-3}y^2+\dots+y^{n-1} \equiv nx^{n-1} \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

The fact that <math>x^n-y^n = (x-y)(x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}y+x^{n-3}y^2+\dots+y^{n-1})</math> completes the proof. The condition <math>\nu_p(x^n+y^n) = \nu_p(x+y)</math> for odd <math>n</math> is similar, where we observe that the proof above holds for integers <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, and therefore we can substitute <math>-y</math> for <math>y</math> above to obtain the desired result.

=== General case (odd ''p'') ===
Via the [[binomial theorem|binomial expansion]], the substitution <math>y = x+kp</math> can be used in ({{EquationNote|1}}) to show that <math>\nu_p(x^p-y^p) = \nu_p(x-y)+1</math> because the quantity in ({{EquationNote|1}}) is a multiple of <math>p</math> but not <math>p^2</math>.<ref name="Parvardi"></ref> Likewise, <math>\nu_p(x^p+y^p) = \nu_p(x+y)+1</math>.

Then, if <math>n</math> is written as <math>p^ab</math> where <math>p \nmid b</math>, the base case gives <math>\nu_p(x^n-y^n) = \nu_p((x^{p^a})^b-(y^{p^a})^b) = \nu_p(x^{p^a}-y^{p^a})</math>. 
By induction on <math>a</math>,
:<math>
\begin{align}
\nu_p(x^{p^a}-y^{p^a}) &= \nu_p(((\dots(x^p)^p\dots))^p-((\dots(y^p)^p\dots))^p)\ \text{(exponentiation used } a \text{ times per term)} \\
&= \nu_p(x-y)+a
\end{align}
</math>

A similar argument can be applied for <math>\nu_p(x^n+y^n)</math>.

=== General case (''p'' = 2) ===
The proof for the odd <math>p</math> case cannot be directly applied when <math>p = 2</math> because the [[binomial coefficient]] <math>\binom{p}{2} = \frac{p(p-1)}{2}</math> is only an integral multiple of <math>p</math> when <math>p</math> is odd.

However, it can be shown that <math>\nu_2(x^n-y^n) = \nu_2(x-y)+\nu_2(n)</math> when <math>4 \mid x-y</math> by writing <math>n = 2^ab</math> where <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are integers with <math>b</math> odd and noting that
:<math>
\begin{align}
\nu_2(x^n-y^n) &= \nu_2((x^{2^a})^b-(y^{2^a})^b) \\
&= \nu_2(x^{2^a}-y^{2^a}) \\
&= \nu_2((x^{2^{a-1}}+y^{2^{a-1}})(x^{2^{a-2}}+y^{2^{a-2}})\cdots(x^2+y^2)(x+y)(x-y)) \\
&= \nu_2(x-y)+a
\end{align}
</math>
because <math>x \equiv y \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{4}</math> implies that each factor of the form <math>x^{2^k}+y^{2^k}</math> in the difference-of-squares step is congruent to 2 modulo 4.

The stronger statement <math>\nu_2(x^n-y^n) = \nu_2(x-y)+\nu_2(x+y)+\nu_2(n)-1</math> when <math>2 \mid x-y</math> is proven analogously.<ref name="Parvardi"/>

== Example problem ==
Problem 12 of the March 2020 [[American Invitational Mathematics Examination|AIME]]:
<blockquote>
Let <math>n</math> be the least positive integer for which <math>149^n-2^n</math> is divisible by <math>3^3\cdot5^5\cdot7^7</math>. Find the number of positive integer divisors of <math>n</math>.<ref>https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php?title=2020_AIME_I_Problems/Problem_12</ref>
</blockquote>

=== Solution ===
Note that <math>149-2 = 147 = 3\cdot 7^2</math>.

Using the lifting-the-exponent lemma, since <math>3 \nmid 149</math> and <math>3 \nmid 2</math>, but <math>3 \mid 147</math>, <math>\nu_3(149^n-2^n) = \nu_3(147)+\nu_3(n) = \nu_3(n)+1</math>. Thus, <math>3^3 \mid 149^n-2^n \iff 3^2 \mid n</math>.

Similarly, <math>7 \nmid 149,2</math> but <math>7 \mid 147</math>, so <math>\nu_7(149^n-2^n) = \nu_7(147)+\nu_7(n) = \nu_7(n)+2</math> and <math>7^7 \mid 149^n-2^n \iff 7^5 \mid n</math>.

Since <math>5 \nmid 147</math>, the factors of 5 are addressed by noticing that since the residues of <math>149^n</math> modulo 5 follow the cycle <math>4,1,4,1</math> and those of <math>2^n</math> follow the cycle <math>2,4,3,1</math>, the residues of <math>149^n-2^n</math> modulo 5 cycle through the sequence <math>2,2,1,0</math>. Thus, <math>5 \mid 149^n-2^n</math> iff <math>n = 4k</math> for some positive integer <math>k</math>. The lemma can now be applied again: <math>\nu_5(149^{4k}-2^{4k}) = \nu_5((149^4)^k-(2^4)^k) = \nu_5(149^4-2^4)+\nu_5(k)</math>. Since <math>149^4-2^4 \equiv (-1)^4-2^4 \equiv -15 \pmod{25}</math>, <math>\nu_5(149^4-2^4) = 1</math>. Hence <math>5^5 \mid 149^n-2^n \iff 5^4 \mid k \iff 4\cdot 5^4 \mid n</math>.

Combining these three results, it is found that <math>n = 2^2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^4\cdot 7^5</math>, which has <math>(2+1)(2+1)(4+1)(5+1) = 270</math> positive divisors.
